authors: Jacobs GH, Birch DG, Blakeslee B
title: Visual acuity and spatial contrast sensitivity in tree squirrels
journal: Behavioural Processes 7: 367-375 (volume as Petry et al. 1984 cite it; the Blakeslee lab page lists volume 1)
why: The only behavioural acuity for tree squirrels, which a later paper describes as low and similar to the tree shrew's 1.2 to 2.4 cycles per degree; would replace the squirrel view's guessed 4.

authors: Vaney DI
title: The grating acuity of the wild European rabbit
why: Behavioural acuity for the wild rabbit; would replace the rabbit view's guessed 3 cycles per degree.

authors: Hughes A
title: The topography of vision in mammals of contrasting life style: comparative optics and retinal organisation
journal: Handbook of Sensory Physiology, Vol. 7 (Crescitelli F, ed.), pp. 613-756, Springer-Verlag
why: Classic measurements of visual fields and streaks in rabbits, ungulates and rodents; would replace the deer's book-sourced 310 degrees and the squirrel's guessed field. Citation read in the reference list of Caves et al. 2018 (reference 10); no DOI seen.

authors: Wallace DJ, Greenberg DS, Sawinski J, Rulla S, Notaro G, Kerr JN
title: Rats maintain an overhead binocular field at the expense of constant fusion
why: How freely moving rats use their overhead binocular field; decides how the mouse view draws the overlap above.

authors: Jacobs GH, Blakeslee B, McCourt ME, Tootell RBH
title: Visual sensitivity of ground squirrels to spatial and temporal luminance variations
why: Behavioural spatial acuity and flicker limits for ground squirrels in one study; would set both the squirrel view's sharpness and its pace for ground squirrels from behaviour instead of from retinal recordings.

authors: Timney B, Keil K
title: Visual acuity in the horse
why: The original of the horse acuity now read through two reviews (about 20/30 on average, best 23.3 cycles per degree); would confirm the conditions behind the horse view's sharpness.

authors: Entsu S, Dohi H, Yamada A
title: Visual acuity of cattle determined by the method of discrimination learning
why: The primary cattle acuity behind a review's 2.6 to 5 cycles per degree; would confirm that cattle and bison belong with deer.

authors: Van Hof MW
title: Visual acuity in the rabbit
why: A second behavioural rabbit acuity to set beside Vaney 1980.

authors: Tansley K, Copenhaver RM, Gunkel RD
title: Some aspects of the electroretinographic response of the American red squirrel, Tamiasciurus hudsonicus loquax
journal: J Cell Compar Physl 57: 11-19 (abbreviation as given in the citing paper)
why: The original of every squirrel flicker value used (L5 to L11) and of the tree-against-ground difference that sets the squirrel view's pace. Citation read in the reference list of Inger et al. 2014 (reference 75); no DOI seen.

authors: Harman AM, Moore S, Hoskins R, Keller P
title: Horse vision and an explanation for the visual behaviour originally explained by the 'ramp retina'
why: The size and place of the horse's blind areas in degrees, for the horse view's blind patch (the 65 to 80 degree overlap is now known from a review).

authors: Hebel R
title: Distribution of retinal ganglion cells in five mammalian species (pig, sheep, ox, horse, dog)
why: Ganglion-cell maps for ox, sheep and horse; gives the streak shape and an anatomical acuity for cattle.

authors: Veilleux CC, Kirk EC
title: Visual acuity in mammals: effects of eye size and ecology
why: A compilation of mammal acuities that probably holds values for squirrels, rabbits and several hoofed animals. Citation read in the reference list of Caves et al. 2018 (reference 15); no DOI seen.

authors: Van Hooser SD, Nelson SB
title: The squirrel as a rodent model of the human visual system
why: Review of squirrel acuity, visual field and timing; may settle the squirrel view's field and sharpness.

authors: Banks MS, et al.
title: Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?
why: Open access but did not load in this session; read directly it would move the pupil and level-eyes rows from g to m and give the rotation range.

authors: D'Angelo GJ, Glasser A, Wendt M, Williams GA, Osborn DA, Gallagher GR, Warren RJ, Miller KV, Pardue MT
title: Visual specialization of an herbivore prey species, the white-tailed deer
why: Cone densities and eye dimensions for an anatomical acuity of the white-tailed deer and the exact shape of its streak.

authors: Jacobs GH, Neitz J, Deegan JF
title: Retinal receptors in rodents maximally sensitive to ultraviolet light
why: Which rodents have ultraviolet cones; decides which mouse-view members keep the ultraviolet tint.

authors: Sugnaseelan S, Prescott NB, Broom DM, Wathes CM, Phillips CJC
title: Visual discrimination learning and spatial acuity in sheep
why: Probably the source of a review's 'up to 14 cycles per degree' for sheep, against Landolt scores of about 2.6 to 5.7; decides whether sheep stay with the deer view.

authors: Lane RH, Allman JM, Kaas JH
title: Representation of the visual field in the superior colliculus of the grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) and the tree shrew (Tupaia glis)
why: Maps the grey squirrel's visual field in the midbrain, which should give the field's extent and its binocular part; the squirrel view's 300 degrees is a guess.

authors: Jacobs GH
title: Spectral sensitivity and colour vision in the ground-dwelling sciurids: results from golden mantled ground squirrels and comparisons for five species
why: Behavioural colour vision in five ground squirrels; would confirm the ground squirrel colour setting.

authors: Jacobs GH, Deegan JF, Neitz J
title: Photopigment basis for dichromatic color vision in cows, goats, and sheep
why: Per-species cone peaks for cattle, goats and sheep (the abstract gives ranges).

authors: Collewijn H
title: The normal range of horizontal eye movements in the rabbit
why: How far a rabbit's eyes move; sets the forward-look vergence effect.

authors: Akaishi Y, Uchiyama H, Ito H, Shimizu Y
title: A morphological study of the retinal ganglion cells of the Afghan pika (Ochotona rufescens)
why: The only pika retina in the collection; tests whether pikas fit the rabbit view.

authors: Mass AM, Supin AYa
title: Estimates of underwater and aerial visual acuity in the European beaver Castor fiber L. based on morphological data
why: Whether the beaver's 17 arcmin is a cycle or a stripe, which doubles or halves its sharpness.
